```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(spLeakage)
```

## A comparison score is a comparison score

`estimate_optimism()` retains its historical name for compatibility. It fits a
learner under the supplied split and a comparison scheme, then reports the
difference between their scores. This difference is evidence of sensitivity to
the validation scheme. It does not establish which score is the error for the
intended deployment target.

Use the same learner, response and loss for both schemes. The package's default
learner is a coordinate-based interpolator; it is not a replacement for an
analyst's ecological prediction model. Here we explicitly supply linear regression
to make the model being compared visible.

```{r example}
set.seed(18)
d <- data.frame(x = runif(120), y = runif(120))
d$z <- 2 * d$x - d$y + rnorm(120, sd = 0.4)
folds <- sample(rep_len(1:5, nrow(d)))
predict_linear <- function(train, test) {
  as.numeric(predict(lm(z ~ x + y, data = train), newdata = test))
}
comparison <- estimate_optimism(d, folds, response = "z", coords = c("x", "y"),
  control = "block", predict_fun = predict_linear)
comparison
```

The historical `optimism` field is the comparison score minus the user-split
score. A blocked or target-matched score has not been declared true deployment
error. Training sizes, covariate support and the learner's dependence on nearby
responses can all affect the difference.

For binary probabilities, Brier loss is squared probability error and log loss is
another appropriate choice. Squared error is also a valid loss for a binary
response; its interpretation depends on the prediction being a probability.
Changing the scoring rule does not establish the validity of the comparison
scheme as a reference.

## Legacy rescaling and simulation emulation

`deleak_estimate()` returns a legacy score comparison with descriptive resampling
intervals. Resampling losses from spatially dependent observations does not by
itself provide a calibrated interval for target risk. Its `reported` argument
rescales a supplied score using the comparison; that calculation must not be
presented as corrected accuracy for a published model.

`predict_optimism()` is a simulation-calibrated emulator retained for research.
Its training learners, data-generating settings, feature construction and
calibration procedure restrict its interpretation. An internal applicability
check does not prove transport to a new ecological model or establish interval
coverage there. It is outside the focused methodological paper and is not used
to support general accuracy correction.

## Ranking and independent validation

`rank_cv_schemes()` defaults to the unsigned Wasserstein distance between
validation and target nearest-neighbour distributions. Alternative signed
criteria are available for explicit comparisons, but a small signed contrast
can result from cancellation. Report the criterion and candidate schemes.

A separate target evaluation can provide evidence that a CV scheme estimates the
relevant error. Its interpretation still depends on how validation locations
were selected and whether their responses were excluded from model fitting and
selection. Repeated partitions of a single survey are not independent datasets.

`design_validation()` is an experimental location-placement heuristic. Its
spatially spread selections do not have known inclusion probabilities, and the
returned stratum weights do not turn it into a probability survey. Its theoretical
allocation comparison omits correlation between prediction errors. Design-based
accuracy assessment requires a separately justified sampling design and estimator.

Report the prediction target, learner, loss, sampling assumptions, training sizes,
observed score comparisons and the limits of any independent evaluation. None of
these legacy function names changes what the underlying computation establishes.
